item.content:encoded:
Ukrainian drone maker General Cherry produces nearly 100,000 drones a month, with interceptor drones costing about $2,000 to shoot down Russian Shaheds worth over $50,000. AI guidance is battle-tested, but full autonomy remains distant.

This episode offers a rare, direct account from a top Ukrainian drone maker of the real forms, costs, and AI limits of battlefield drones. Dense with information, it is directly valuable for understanding modern warfare and the drone industry.

4:07 Producing nearly 100,000 a month, capacity still expanding
General Cherry was founded in 2023, initially producing only about 10 drones a month. Now monthly output reaches about 100,000 (exact figure undisclosed). The company works with more than 110 military brigades, and the best units consume over 5,000 drones a month. Capacity is still growing because battlefield consumption is enormous—drones have become expendables.

7:09 Hundreds of drone companies in Ukraine, but only 10–15 at the top
Ukraine may have as many as 2,000 drone companies, but the vast majority are garage-style small workshops. Only 10 to 15 large companies can produce 1,000 to 10,000 a month, and General Cherry claims to be in the top five. This fragmented yet vast industrial ecosystem is the basis for Ukraine's rapid innovation, but it also means intense competition.

8:14 AI models developed in-house, co-created deeply with the military
General Cherry's AI guidance system is fully self-developed, backed by a strong R&D department, and built in close cooperation with different frontline units. They gather battlefield feedback daily through mobile teams and iterate products quickly. This closed loop of R&D–combat–feedback lets Ukrainian drone tech adapt rapidly to the battlefield, rather than relying on external procurement.

10:20 Rocket-shaped FPVs come from Red Bull, not Ukraine
This rocket-shaped FPV drone is not a Ukrainian original; it was first used by Red Bull in 2021 or 2022 for sports events. Ukrainian companies found the shape could reach higher speeds than ordinary quadcopters, so they adopted and optimized it. This reflects the fast-learning, pragmatic nature of Ukraine's drone industry—not chasing originality, only effectiveness.

17:24 A $2,000 interceptor drone against a $50,000 Shahed
General Cherry's interceptor drones (such as the Bullet) cost about $2,000, yet can shoot down Russian Shahed drones that cost $50,000 to $100,000. This asymmetric cost exchange is a key strategy against Russia's saturation attacks—using cheap drones to exhaust expensive enemy assets while avoiding wasting Western-supplied expensive air-defense missiles.

21:28 Interceptors confirmed to have downed over 5,000 Russian aircraft
General Cherry's tactical interceptor drones (General Trajectory Air) have confirmed over 5,000 Russian drone kills since production began in February 2025, with over 1,000 Russian Moniya drones downed in December alone. The Shahed-interceptor model also entered mass production in December 2025, with confirmed kills nearing 1,000. These numbers show interceptors have become a significant force in battlefield air defense.

23:28 AI runs on-device, not in the cloud
General Cherry's AI guidance model runs on the drone's local camera chip, not in the cloud. The operator detects the target via radar, launches the drone, and the AI automatically identifies and locks on without human intervention. This edge AI design avoids battlefield communication latency and jamming, which is key to being practical in combat.

27:32 Fully autonomous weapons are a terrifying future, but AI is inevitable
Marko admits that if drones become fully autonomous, it will be terrifying—killing would no longer require another person, just a robot or drone. Currently they use semi-autonomous AI only on interceptor drones, because adding AI to ordinary FPVs significantly raises cost, making it better to buy more non-AI drones. But he predicts AI technology will spread quickly and prices will drop, making future battlefields even more brutal.

item.title: Land Is Not a Commodity: Why a Land Value Tax Can Cure the Housing Crisis
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-moneymacro-土地不是商品-地价税为何能根治住房危机/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-moneymacro-土地不是商品-地价税为何能根治住房危机/
item.description: The housing shortage is just the surface; the real disease is land monopoly: a land value tax shifts the burden from buildings to land, forcing hoarders to develop or sell, returning location value to society instead of enriching landlords.
item.content:encoded:
The housing shortage is just the surface; the real disease is land monopoly: a land value tax shifts the burden from buildings to land, forcing hoarders to develop or sell, returning location value to society instead of enriching landlords.

The land value tax is an overlooked lever that economists on both left and right agree on. Lars Doucet uses cases like Houston parking lots, Korea's assessment system, and Norway's resource dividends to turn an abstract tax into a story of power struggle.

0:05 A land tax is not a property tax; it's a location tax
Lars sets up his argument with an analogy: the land value tax shares a root with ordinary property tax, but it splits 'building value' from 'land value.' A building tax punishes you for building, maintaining, and renovating; a land tax only punishes you for occupying a prime location and letting it sit idle. He says land's value comes from the labor of the people around you—the fact that you can step out your door to work, study, and make friends depends on your neighbors and the whole city. Landlords lie back and siphon this collective value into their own pockets. This is the paradox of 'Progress and Poverty': a ballpoint pen fell from $270 to 11 cents, but land never does that.

0:13 The build-more crowd is right, but not enough
The host asks: Oakland relaxed density and rents fell—do we still need a land tax? Lars admits the 'housing shortage' is the main cause, but he points out that the YIMBYs don't explain a counterexample: Houston has no zoning, yet downtown still has a giant surface parking lot worth $500 million. Why? Because the property tax bundles land and buildings together; the more you build, the more you pay, while hoarding and waiting for appreciation is cheaper. So developers have no incentive to develop, only to lobby for rezoning and then keep hoarding. He says that without land tax reform, you end up in a stalemate: 'You changed the zoning, but I still won't sell.'

0:23 The objections are born of imagination
Lars groups the objections into three categories and dismantles each. How do you separate land from buildings in assessment? He says about 14,000 assessment jurisdictions worldwide already do something similar; Korea manually reviews 500,000 sample parcels every year and produces a nationwide land value map in five months; Norway trains a national automated valuation model on the Finn.no property data platform, with a core team of just three people. Worried about protests? He says the real source of protest is 'my land looks the same as my neighbor's, why do I pay more?' Under a land tax, your assessment basis is the same location as your neighbor's, so it's actually easier to calculate. The excuse for not implementing is that it hasn't been measured.

0:35 Little old ladies are not a reason to object
The sharpest criticism is 'transition unfairness'—the day a land tax is announced, existing landowners instantly bear the capitalized burden of all future taxes, a one-time expropriation. Lars acknowledges this is a Gordon Tullock-style transition trap, then offers safeguards: action is never a one-step nationwide 100% land tax, but a gradual switch by school district or county; run revenue-neutral simulations, and most single-family homes see their tax bills fall. As for the elderly worried about being driven out of their homes, he says Texas already has a tax deferral system: you owe it, and after death it's deducted from the estate with interest.

0:41 Britain's failure is a capacity problem
The most common counterexample online is Britain's 1910 'People's Budget': valuation took six years and was overturned by shopkeeper protests and the courts. Lars's response is blunt: the much-discussed article is 'inferring a universal law from one sample,' and it simultaneously claims 'a pure land tax has never succeeded' and 'land cannot be valued'—yet Korea has been assessing the entire national land value parcel by parcel for decades. He says this only proves Britain's state capacity was weak, not that the land tax is theoretically unworkable. His tone turns serious: if you want to be a serious critic, go find counterexamples, don't pass off lazy ignorance as settled truth.

0:45 Norway achieves Georgism through resource dividends
Lars points to a fact that makes Norway a 'success story' today: the entire Norwegian resource management system is Georgist in structure—oil and other natural resources are deemed the property of all the people, extractors pay extremely high resource taxes, but production and investment themselves are not penalized. This encourages entrepreneurship while channeling the natural dividend into the state treasury to subsidize universal welfare. Norway's Georgism is almost perfect, except it doesn't apply to land value tax. This 'Norwegian paradox' leads him to assert: the land tax is not the enemy of the welfare state; it can be its foundation.

0:51 The automobile opened a second frontier
Lars explains why the land question that filled the air 100 years ago later disappeared: the frontier itself was a kind of 'free land' mechanism—as long as you could expand into the wilderness, the lower classes didn't have to face the squeeze of 'high work plus high rent.' America's first frontier was the westward movement; after it closed came Henry George. In the 20th century, the automobile turned the suburbs into a 'second frontier,' extending the reprieve for another 80 years, until it closed again around 2006–2008. He says some now call this the 'Second Gilded Age,' but it's just the same script from a hundred years ago with a new cast, and post-pandemic remote work as a 'third frontier' lasted only about five minutes before capital absorbed it.

0:53 Don't win online; do homework for politicians
The closing answer is practical: Lars says the most effective way to create change he's learned in the past five years is not arguing with keyboard warriors, but preparing data simulations and ready-made responses to every objection a state senator or city councilor might raise, and putting them directly on their desks—he calls 'doing homework for politicians' an absurd but remarkably effective strategy. Today several states have passed bills allowing land value tax reform. His action advice: go measure, don't guess.

item.title: What Drives Founders Isn't Becoming a Billionaire—It's Fear of the Server Crashing at 3 AM
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-ycsp-驱动创始人的不是当亿万富翁-是怕服务器半夜崩掉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-ycsp-驱动创始人的不是当亿万富翁-是怕服务器半夜崩掉/
item.description: Most people think wealth ambition gets you through a startup. Paul Graham says what actually pushes you forward day to day is disaster fear—the server crashing, the toy train about to fall off the table. You keep your head down fixing trains for ten years, look up, and realize you're already a billionaire at the last round's valuation.
item.content:encoded:
Most people think wealth ambition gets you through a startup. Paul Graham says what actually pushes you forward day to day is disaster fear—the server crashing, the toy train about to fall off the table. You keep your head down fixing trains for ten years, look up, and realize you're already a billionaire at the last round's valuation.

After 21 years and 47 batches, PG's take: AI has barely changed anything about startups—only the bill. Good for calibrating your confidence in 'this time is different.'

2:02 Nostalgia for the golden age forgets it only had Reddit
People have been saying YC is past its prime since around 2008. PG reads this as: attackers must first admit it was once great, so they can only say 'it's not what it used to be.' His counterexample is concrete: the representative product of the so-called good era was Reddit, while this episode's office hours included intercontinental ballistic freight—like an ICBM, except instead of exploding on landing, it unloads cargo. Another category is curing cancer. He says there are too many approaches—vaccines on one end, therapies on the other—so you should invest in several; any one succeeding makes it worth it. One company in this episode does on-demand research for cancer patients, and he likes exactly that approach: cancer is famously not solved by 'coming up with one cure'; maybe the way to beat it is death by a thousand cuts.

4:09 Google won't be breached; it will be obsoleted by the world
Many ideas from the 2012 'frighteningly ambitious' essay have already been done, including 'a new Google.' PG says he predicted the path back then: you can't attack Google head-on; you wait for the world to change until its model is obsolete. OpenAI is that change itself—after using it, he no longer uses search, because what he always wanted wasn't web pages but information, so he just asks AI. This is a corollary that applies to all incumbents: moats aren't breached; they're obsoleted.

6:15 Ambition is the entry ticket; daily fuel is fear of looking bad
Ambition is necessary because startup obstacles are too terrifying to get through on conscientiousness alone. But PG says what actually moves a founder at any given moment isn't 'solve this and I'll be a billionaire'—it's disaster fear: the server crashing, fear of looking like a fool. His image is a toy train—the engine is about to fall off the table edge, and you rush to catch it. You spend ten years head-down fixing trains, look up at the last round's valuation, and realize you're already a billionaire. He says sometimes he's the one who calculates it first and tells the founder.

9:21 The only test of formidable is getting what you want
Formidable was a private word PG and Jessica used before YC. His definition is operational: this person can get what they want in any situation—if they can't, how are they formidable? This definition also explains the investment logic: you hold stock in their company, they hold it too, interests are aligned; they get what they want, you get what you want. It's also a precondition for his answer to where the next trillion-dollar company comes from.

11:24 Lean startup isn't dead: even rocket companies can start small
Asked whether lean startup is dead and you now have to burn big money from day one, PG's rebuttal has two layers. First, price: tokens are expensive now only because of GPU shortage; the price for the same level of reasoning drops about 30x per year, and you're also getting higher-quality tokens—technology always gets cheaper. Second, path: even rocket companies can start with modest money. You can't build a real rocket, but you can build the design, run simulations, show experts, and if it's convincing enough you get the next round. StarCloud wrote a white paper and booked one launch—though he added that the founder is a known expert in the field with built-in credibility; a fresh graduate won't have it so easy.

13:24 AI went the wrong way: from human toward perfect
In the 1980s, AI people thought the path was from 'perfect fly'—doing only fly things but doing them as well as a fly—then climbing up to mouse, cat, monkey, human, each level perfect. What they got was the reverse—a full human right away, but one that talks nonsense, like an undergrad trying to bluff through a paper. What got optimized was the opposite dimension: not from perfect toward human, but from human toward perfect. This also explains the jagged frontier: it can solve math problems but can't answer what time a restaurant opens.

16:30 AI changes the bill structure, not the shipping speed
PG says the best predictor of startup success is still shipping speed, and AI hasn't replaced that metric—with these tools in hand, plenty of companies in this episode still don't ship fast enough, showing the difference isn't in how fast you can write things; you first have to come up with the ideas. 'With AI, what hasn't changed?' His answer: so far almost everything is exactly the same. The only strange new thing is the bill structure—before, the big cost of a startup was salaries, everything else was cheap by comparison; now there's GPU, and tokens can burn tens of thousands of dollars a day.

19:36 The next trillion-dollar company comes from the right people, not the right idea
Asked where the next trillion-dollar company will come from, PG switches the question from sector to people: it comes from the right founder, not a specific idea—startup ideas are highly variable, and he'll only say 'probably not dog walking.' Conversely, to judge whether a company is worth investing in, first judge whether the founder is formidable; what they're working on is likely promising. As for whether future founders will look different, he says there's already 20 years of data: today's founders are exactly the same as 20 years ago, and there's no reason they'll change in the next 20.

item.title: Arm Goes Down to Make CPUs: The Biggest Bottleneck in Chip Design Is Verification, Not Design
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-nopriors-arm-下场造-cpu-芯片设计最大瓶颈是验证-不是设计/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-nopriors-arm-下场造-cpu-芯片设计最大瓶颈是验证-不是设计/
item.description: The real time sink in the chip cycle is verification, debugging, and documentation, not RTL; Arm already has 80%-90% of engineers using AI daily, and has broken its 98.5% gross margin licensing model to make CPUs itself.
item.content:encoded:
The real time sink in the chip cycle is verification, debugging, and documentation, not RTL; Arm already has 80%-90% of engineers using AI daily, and has broken its 98.5% gross margin licensing model to make CPUs itself.

Get Arm's internal real data on AI's usefulness in chip design, then see product, capital, and supply chain judgments form a closed loop—worth benchmarking for AI infrastructure practitioners.

3:43 Arm's move to make CPUs itself is customer demand
Arm originally only sold IP licenses with a 98.5% gross margin, never touching inventory or wafers. The step forward to compute subsystems already had customers grabbing the pre-integrated 'subsystems' of CPU, GPU, and memory as modules. Going further is because 'customers wanting general-purpose CPUs for the large-model era can't find a supplier' and came directly to Arm. Before the announcement, they asked nearly all licensees; opposition was minimal: a bigger software ecosystem benefits every customer, so Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google—companies making Arm server chips—all publicly supported it.

8:07 Banning AI tools is like sending engineers back to the library
The total chip design cycle is 24-36 months; the most time-consuming part is not RTL generation or architecture mapping, but verification, validation, debugging, and documentation. AI is especially suited to these tasks. Internally, about 80%-90% of Arm engineers already use AI daily; turning off the tools would be like in the 1990s letting people use the internet only two hours a day and sending them back to the library downstairs for the rest. Currently AI's weakest areas are RTL generation and physical design, because models rely on public corpora while the industry's most critical details are private data—exactly the gap companies like Arm can fill.

10:35 From idea to tapeout is five years away, not two or three
The host asked: if AI eats the most time-consuming verification step, can the 24-36 months shrink to 6-12? Rene Haas gave a measured answer: 2-3 years is unrealistic; beyond five years, for designs with less complex constraints, going from idea all the way to GDSII (the tapeout file handed to the foundry) is possible. If you feed the tool 'make a chip 10% faster, 20% cheaper, 30% more power-efficient than a reference,' don't expect a one-click finish. His judgment: in 5-10 years, the industry's design methodology will change markedly.

15:00 AI supply and demand are far apart; the bottleneck is construction sites, not wafers
Discussing the AI bubble, Rene Haas distinguished between stock-level valuation froth and the industry chain itself; he stated clearly that supply 'is far from' demand. Transformer inference and training consume both compute and memory, so demand won't stop. The real hard constraint will shift to data center construction: many projects are being delayed and need more manpower, and there is growing resistance to new data centers in various places. In the next 3-5 years, the constraint may not be wafer capacity or memory, but the persistently tight physical construction.

17:14 SoftBank's cloud move gives chip companies a customer
For chip/AI entrepreneurs in heavy-asset, high-capex businesses: capital availability itself is a gate, and strategic partnerships should reach the supply chain, PE, and bank levels early. Behind Arm is SoftBank, not just as a shareholder; SoftBank just announced it will build a 'neo cloud' type service, so young chip companies don't have to only knock on Microsoft's or Google's door for design wins—they can form a direct customer relationship with the Arm/SoftBank ecosystem, adding another path to market.

21:25 Humanoids won't unify; specialized robots will coexist long-term
Rene Haas believes robot 1.0 is purpose-built: both mechanics and software are optimized for a single action, and changing a production line almost means starting over. New-generation robots that can redefine tasks through training and have general-purpose mechanical bodies will first eat repetitive labor in construction, infrastructure, and security. Form factors won't converge on a single direction: factories, warehouses, and tools are all designed to human dimensions, so humanoids have an advantage; other tasks are better suited to specialized forms. Costs must come down first, and delivery and warehousing will be the earliest automation scenarios.

27:13 Curbing chip exports to China is an unwinnable infinite game
He is direct on US manufacturing: America should build more fabs domestically, for both national security and supply chain diversification. On export controls, he speaks of an 'infinite game'—restricting chip exports to China cannot produce a finite victory, and may instead drive key technologies out of the US. He also denies that data centers are 'big warehouses with no jobs': the ecosystem around energy, liquid cooling, etc., can create jobs in America.

36:00 In the token world, every path goes through the CPU
Using the token factory metaphor for accelerators, Rene Haas thinks the real system question is: who orchestrates and arbitrates where tokens go, and delivers them to users? He believes every path goes through the CPU: beyond training, there is inference scheduling, system orchestration, context and tool invocation. At the edge, on devices that can't fit a 50W GPU, Arm's power advantage is more pronounced. The CPU hasn't disappeared; instead, it creates sustained demand alongside accelerators.

item.title: The Top Warning Sign of Financial Fraud: Not Greed, but Personal Financial Trouble
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-rationalreminder-金融舞弊头号预警-不是贪婪-是个人财务先失控/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-rationalreminder-金融舞弊头号预警-不是贪婪-是个人财务先失控/
item.description: For 14 consecutive years, the ACFE has ranked "personal financial issues" as the top red flag for financial misconduct; systemic incentives, a shutdown of critical brain regions, and moral overconfidence can all push good people across the line step by step.
item.content:encoded:
For 14 consecutive years, the ACFE has ranked "personal financial issues" as the top red flag for financial misconduct; systemic incentives, a shutdown of critical brain regions, and moral overconfidence can all push good people across the line step by step.

The two authors—one a clinical neuropsychologist, the other with 20 years of experience prosecuting financial advisors—offer a profile of wrongdoers and warning signs that are more useful for screening than moral slogans.

2:04 The test for crossing the line is: this is not your money
Moira defines financial misconduct as "doing bad things with other people's money"—both taking money for oneself and guiding or advising others to use funds in ways that are not in their best interest. She stresses that anyone working in finance must constantly remember "this is not your money." Framing the ethical problem as fiduciary duty gives a unified benchmark for the warning signs that follow.

9:10 For 14 years, the top warning sign has been personal financial trouble
Philippa cites the ACFE's global report: for 14 consecutive years, the number one red flag for fraud has not been greed but "personal financial issues"—people whose personal finances are out of control, who cannot make ends meet, or who are drowning in debt are the most likely to become involved in financial misconduct. The financial industry provides access to others' money, attracts people who seek wealth, and combines with people's irrationality around money—these three conditions stack up to create fertile ground for misconduct.

13:14 When taking advice, the brain is like praying: critical regions go offline
Moira notes that neuroimaging evidence shows that when people receive financial advice, key critical regions of the brain "go offline," a state similar to the brain during prayer. People feel safe, trusting, and open; this non-critical state increases vulnerability, especially for those unfamiliar with finance. She gives the example that even hedge fund managers will "sit and wait for the answer" from an advisor without asking how the product actually works.

19:19 Good people go wrong starting with obedience and helpfulness, not greed
Philippa and Moira dissect the path by which good people err: blindly following orders, crossing lines out of "misguided helpfulness," then hiding mistakes out of fear, and covering with bigger lies. The book's "John" slides from a small mistake to lying, then to doubling down on concealment. Moira emphasizes that ethics is not a solo sport but a team sport; if organizational culture tacitly permits misconduct, individuals find it hard to stay clean.

37:36 Psychopaths disproportionately flow into finance
Responding to Cameron's concern, Moira says the evidence shows that psychopaths disproportionately enter finance and business because "that's where the money is." She cites Robert Hare's research: successful psychopaths are often charming and extremely skilled at detecting and exploiting others' desires. They cause great damage and often continue moving within the industry because colleagues feel "relief" when they leave, passing the problem to the next firm.

53:50 Most people never realize they are making an ethical decision
Traditional ethics training always presents clear moral dilemmas in the classroom, but real-world problems often emerge quietly, so people do not realize they are at a fork in the road. Moira cites Kahneman's "what you see is all there is": people do not actively question the motives of product providers, do not think about who benefits from complex products, and do not admit that they do not actually understand. The result is that even those trained in ethics often do not know they are facing an ethical decision most of the time.

1:02:56 The future wrongdoer is a vulnerable ordinary person, not a villain
Philippa lists the profile of future wrongdoers: early in their career (Evan was drawn into global fraud within a month of joining and was banned for life after nine months), in debt, highly dependent on their boss, with a pleasing personality, low self-esteem (compensating with luxury cars), fatigue, family problems, and so on. These signals are rarely used by the industry to screen advisors' own biases; they are not rare evil but common weaknesses of ordinary people under stress and vulnerability.

1:09:07 After 20 years of prosecutions, never a single CFP holder
Philippa has been a lawyer for 20 years and has prosecuted many financial practitioners, yet she has never prosecuted a single CFP designee. She believes there is no simple way to pick a good advisor, but earning a certification is a positive signal. She also offers a criterion: if an advisor only talks about investments and does not understand the client's whole life situation, that is wealth management, not financial planning—planning is about the person, not the assets.

item.title: US Bond Yields Above 5% Aren't About Inflation: $32 Trillion in Debt Means Buyers Only Accept Higher Prices
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-oddlots-美债利率上-5-不是通胀闹的-32-万亿国债让买家只肯加价接盘/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-oddlots-美债利率上-5-不是通胀闹的-32-万亿国债让买家只肯加价接盘/
item.description: Inflation can't explain the 30-year breaking 5%: even with no inflation and no default risk, buyers already allocated at 5.3% won't bite for another $10 billion. What's really lifting the curve is the $2 trillion in annual supply, and the Treasury's buybacks can't hold it down.
item.content:encoded:
Inflation can't explain the 30-year breaking 5%: even with no inflation and no default risk, buyers already allocated at 5.3% won't bite for another $10 billion. What's really lifting the curve is the $2 trillion in annual supply, and the Treasury's buybacks can't hold it down.

The mainstream narrative blames inflation for the 30-year at 5%; this episode offers a genuinely incremental alternative framework, folding the Treasury's intervention limits, the Fed's balance-sheet mechanics, and the term-premium debate into one logic.

4:04 5% Is First the Treasury's Interest Bill, Not a Macro Signal
Host Joe asks Daryl what he sees when the 30-year Treasury yield is above 5%—even after a slight pullback following the Fed chair's speech. Daryl's answer isn't a macro model but the Treasury's predicament: if I were Treasury secretary, I'd see extremely high interest costs for the US government and would have to find ways to push yields down. That line sets the episode's frame: officials have a strong incentive to suppress long-end rates, but whether they can and should is the premise for everything that follows.

5:07 To Sell Another $10 Billion, the Treasury Must Pay Higher Interest
Daryl offers the episode's core thought experiment: suppose there's no inflation risk and no sovereign default, and you're a macro hedge fund already holding $20 billion in 10-year Treasuries. The Treasury secretary calls and asks you to buy another $10 billion—why would you refuse? The answer: you've already made your desired allocation at a 5.3% yield; to get you to add more, they must pay a higher rate to compensate. This logic also illustrates the demand-side structural shift—foreign central banks are already fully allocated and no longer buying, so new supply must be absorbed by domestic free discretionary buyers: banks, pensions, insurers, and hedge funds, all highly yield-sensitive.

8:10 It's Not That the Logic Changed; Debt Has Hit a Tipping Point
Joe raises the objection that must be faced: the bearish logic of aging populations, political unwillingness to cut spending, and unsustainable deficits existed in 2018 and 2019, and Japan was told the same story for decades—so why did yields fall then but rise now? Daryl's answer is scale: the IMF's old 60% debt-to-GDP red line is far in the rearview mirror, with France already at 100%; the US Treasury market has grown from about $18 trillion to $31 trillion and keeps expanding. There's no new logic; the sheer quantity of debt has accumulated to a tipping point.

10:13 The Long End at 5% Is Driven by Supply, Not Inflation Expectations
Given that the short end is still constrained by high inflation and the Fed, why can't the 30-year's high yield be directly attributed to inflation expectations? Daryl acknowledges that inflation over the past five years has indeed been significantly above the Fed's target and that hitting the target is still incomplete, but he points out: the implied inflation expectations derived from real and nominal bonds aren't flashing alarm; investors actually trading 10-, 20-, and 30-year Treasuries are processing supply relative to demand first, not inflation. He mentions John Cochrane's fiscal theory of the price level, but that's a long-run framework—the current driver of term premia is issuance, not prices.

13:18 Buybacks to Cap Yields Are Just a Signal; Ammunition Is Far Too Thin
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an expansion of Treasury buybacks, with the official rationale being liquidity. Daryl reads between the lines directly: from his public remarks, he doesn't think the problem is market liquidity; he thinks yields are 'too high' and says outright he's sending a signal to the market. The problem is that the scale of Treasury operations is a drop in the bucket relative to the entire Treasury market; the market moved briefly on the news and then quickly reversed. Trying to use government resources to suppress yield trends has a precedent in the 1992 pound sterling attack—and Bessent was one of the people shorting sterling at Soros's fund back then.

19:22 Buybacks' Real Job Is Cleaning Up Old Bonds, Not Managing Rates
The original design of the buyback program wasn't to manage yields: as the Treasury keeps issuing new bonds, the market accumulates a large amount of off-the-run bonds that have lost liquidity, clogging dealer balance sheets and distorting prices away from a smooth yield curve. Daryl's paper with two New York Fed economists tests whether buying back odd lots at a 'regular, predictable' pace and reissuing new bonds can improve market liquidity and earn taxpayers a buy-low-sell-high profit. The term 'odd lots' is exactly where the show gets its name. He thinks this routine operation is effective, but the Treasury stepping in to defend its own bond market in an emergency is a different matter.

25:30 The Constraint on Shrinking the Balance Sheet Is Reserves, Not Assets
The new Fed chair wants to shrink the balance sheet, but most people only watch the asset side. Daryl points out the arithmetic constraint: selling assets requires an equal reduction in liabilities. Of the three liability components, the TGA can't have the Treasury withdraw its deposits, and currency in circulation can't be recalled; the only compressible piece is bank reserves held at the Fed. But today's reserves are the 'Swiss Army knife' of the financial system: they earn interest at market rates, satisfy liquidity regulation, and are always available for payments—banks have no incentive to give them up. The ratchet effect that Acharya and Rajan described at Jackson Hole in 2017 already showed that every time the Fed expands, banks become addicted to reserves, and shrinking inevitably causes market volatility.

28:33 The Task Force Will Swap Durations, Not Truly Shrink
Daryl says he has no inside information on the task force, but he makes two predictions about the group led by Jeremy Stein: first, the real problem is structure, not size—the sensible approach is to gradually replace long-term Treasuries with short-term bills, so that interest expense on the liability side (reserves) moves in the same direction as interest income on the asset side (bills), reducing the impact of policy-rate volatility on the Fed's own P&L; second, don't keep mortgage-backed securities on the asset side—let them run off naturally. His own conclusion is blunter: the Fed may not actually need to shrink, but it must have tools to shrink on its own, or it will be backed into a corner when Congress pressures it.

item.title: The Profit Code of Wallets Isn't Balance Interest, It's Money Circulating Within the System
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-complexsys-钱包的利润密码不是余额利息-是钱在体系内流转/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-complexsys-钱包的利润密码不是余额利息-是钱在体系内流转/
item.description: The core accounting of a wallet: money coming in incurs card network fees, internal transfers are nearly free, and withdrawals can be charged again; it earns from the spread of movement, not from idle balances. PayPal, Cash App, and Stripe Link are all betting on this model.
item.content:encoded:
The core accounting of a wallet: money coming in incurs card network fees, internal transfers are nearly free, and withdrawals can be charged again; it earns from the spread of movement, not from idle balances. PayPal, Cash App, and Stripe Link are all betting on this model.

A real breakdown of wallet cost structures: wholesale channel fees are less than a cent, yet platforms can charge users several cents; Japanese peers even open multiple bank accounts to bypass clearing. Even if you're not in payments, this serves as a business teardown template.

1:05 A wallet must answer how it makes money from day one
The episode opens with a $100 Venmo payment to a barber, questioning why PayPal still wants to insert itself into such small transactions that already have mature payment rails. It then quickly defines the scope: this is about e-wallet businesses, not crypto private-key wallets. Because a wallet appears to hold balances, it immediately enters the regulatory sensitive zone of deposits, so from day one a wallet must answer how it makes money—if it can't, the product dies.

5:14 Card fraud isn't from fake websites, it's from issuer-side leaks
The biggest early obstacle to online transactions was users' reluctance to hand over card numbers, with media constantly hyping the risk of card theft. The author points out the opposite is true: much fraud comes from massive data leaks on the issuing side, not from scammers building fake sites, concluding that 'economies of scale also protect criminals.' PayPal's value was to shield users between their card numbers and the payee, limiting the risk of each transaction—this justified charging close to 3% in channel fees and planted the seed for the subsequent balance design.

6:19 A free wallet is anything but free for the wallet itself
Putting money into a wallet requires going through card networks, historically priced around 3%, and this cost is borne by the wallet. But once balances stay within the system, transfers between users are almost like editing a database row—so cheap they can't be billed. PayPal charges near the original price on both ends, so merely substituting internal transfers for external ones yields extra gross margin. A wallet that seems free to the average user is not free for the wallet—the zero marginal cost of existing balances is the real moat.

9:21 Driving down channel fees beats product innovation for profits
There's no inherent link between wholesale and retail: when purchasing millions of ACH transactions, the cost is about $0.05 each, yet payment service providers can charge merchants nearly $0.30; the difference is the tax platforms levy on the underlying rails. Japan is more extreme: interbank transfers cost about ¥200 per transaction, while intra-bank entries are nearly free, so some products open accounts at major banks, move users' money within the bank, and settle via daily netting. In the financial world, reducing channel fees can more directly become wallet profit than product innovation.

12:27 Withdrawals aren't a user perk; they're a second revenue pipe
Cash App prices withdrawals too: for speed, you choose the more expensive card rail, charged at 1.75% with a $0.25 minimum; the author tested withdrawing $50 and was quoted $0.88. Complementing this is a partnership with institutions like Sutton Bank to issue prepaid cards, so spending outside the system also shares in swipe fees. Wallets no longer treat withdrawals as a user benefit but as a second revenue stream, because partner banks need the wallet's user scale, and the wallet needs the bank's issuing license.

20:53 Co-branded cards earn a cut but carry the bad debt
The logic of wallet co-branded credit cards is two-way charging, but risk control is the real battleground: wallets typically assume their accumulated spending data can approve better than issuers. The industry has repeatedly shown that FICO is already so strong it's hard to replace; additional variables that materially improve losses often cross legal red lines. What truly prices the wallet is the agreement—banks require the entire loan portfolio's loss rate to stay below a threshold, otherwise the wallet's revenue share drops to zero or even goes negative. 10-K language avoids 'loss sharing,' but in essence the wallet is absorbing the issuer's bad debt.

24:50 Users care about the phone, not the card
Apple's core argument to banks is that users care about their phones, not the plastic credit card; if banks don't pay up, Apple could support or build a new two-sided payment network and take users with it. Reports say Apple takes 15 basis points per Apple Pay transaction, while Google reportedly takes nothing—the author uses this to mock the two giants' differing abilities in non-core products. The next layer is the conclusion that the checkout itself can be like an ad slot: when the product and price are set, who gets to place the payment method first becomes an auction. Stripe has already changed traditional displays to dynamic sorting based on user preferences, even opening merchant micro-adjustments.

31:13 Channel fees aren't cut at the negotiating table but in default settings
Extending Link as a ledger-level settlement negotiation layer: if users store their low-fee payment methods in Link, the next checkout can bypass card networks and go through bank accounts; the saved channel fees are redistributed between merchants and users. This solution can't be achieved by one company sitting at a table, but by the aggregation of millions of users' and merchants' decisions, ultimately giving the party on the other side of the payment negotiation a scale close to 1% of global GDP. Only this scale can force channel fees to be repriced.

item.title: No Quantum Gravity, No Real AGI
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-spc-解不出量子引力-就不算真正的-agi/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-spc-解不出量子引力-就不算真正的-agi/
item.description: A physicist draws a high bar for AGI: it must solve quantum gravity. This conversation also clarifies the real relationship between quantum materials and AI—after filtering for synthesizability, the discovered materials may number zero.
item.content:encoded:
A physicist draws a high bar for AGI: it must solve quantum gravity. This conversation also clarifies the real relationship between quantum materials and AI—after filtering for synthesizability, the discovered materials may number zero.

A noise-canceling listen for the AI world's default assumptions: a string theorist makes scientific payoffs and AI's limits concrete and testable, useful for calibrating your own timelines in hard tech. The pace is a bit slow; the core arguments cluster in the middle and later sections.

17:28 Too much learning paralyzes; naivety lets you ask raw questions
The hardest step from student to researcher is not absorbing knowledge but posing the raw questions that push the boundary of knowledge forward. Gopakumar describes this leap as "naivety plus experience": learning too much can paralyze you—you need to keep a bit of naive to dare ask questions that seem impossible to approach. A mentor's job is to teach you to break big questions into small steps you can advance today without losing the ultimate goal. His own mentor, David Gross, excelled at this—by Gopakumar's account, Gross's first student produced work that won the Nobel Prize together with the advisor, and Witten also won a Fields Medal. Now he trains his own students with the same method: the first one or two problems are assigned by him, and he himself has no answer; he works through them slowly with students until their third or fourth year, then lets them pose their own questions.

28:36 Spacetime is not a backdrop but an emergent approximation
Use "water made of discrete atoms" to understand string theory: the continuous spacetime we touch is likely a low-resolution approximation of some deeper structure at macroscopic scales. Gopakumar stresses this is not pure speculation—quantum mechanics itself does not allow treating spacetime as an infinitely divisible smooth backdrop; add black holes (which Hawking and others found to have many anomalous properties) and the breakdown at the Big Bang singularity, and physicists must answer where spacetime comes from. String theory offers a natural framework: spacetime emerges from something more fundamental, and gravity along with the known interactions fit inside. This explains why he sets "solving quantum gravity" as a very high bar for intelligence: it demands not just problem-solving but building a new conceptual framework.

39:45 Materials should be designed backward: fix properties first, then find structure
Start with a long-term yardstick: quantum mechanics was initially meant to understand atoms, but the devices it now underpins account, by his estimate, for roughly 35%–40% of US GDP, and the commercial ripple only became visible four to five decades after the theory appeared. He calls the current phase the second quantum revolution: accidentally discovered quantum materials like graphene are already commercializing, and the next step is AI-driven inverse materials design—define what properties a material must have, then search for what structure can realize them and how to synthesize it, bypassing traditional trial-and-error chemistry. He also recounts a conversation with Demis Hassabis: DeepMind's next holy grail is finding a room-temperature superconductor, and Hassabis warned him at the outset not to bring up quantum gravity.

50:59 Getting stuck is the norm; keep three or four problems in play
Being stuck is not the exception but the daily life of a researcher; especially during the transition from student to researcher, being stuck can feel crushing. Gopakumar's first strategy is portfolio hedging: work on three or four problems at once; if one dies, switch to another, and by probability at least one will move half a step. The second is to teach—when students' eyes light up, that satisfaction can pull you out of a low, and he has often found that "after a lecture, a stuck problem suddenly opens up." The third is to deliberately learn something new you have always wanted to study but never had time for, gaining a new frame of reference before returning to the old problem.

55:08 Talent multiplies rather than adds; headcount is never the missing piece
Why does top science concentrate in a few places rather than spread evenly? Gopakumar offers a mechanism: being in the same place, talking, using each other as sounding boards—even without formal collaboration—keeps the brain in a stimulated state; when collaboration does happen, the different skills of two people multiply rather than add. He borrows a physics metaphor: photons in an ordinary bulb are chaotic, while photons in a laser are coherent with each other; once a group forms coherence, it can produce a lasing effect. He says many Indian institutions underperform relative to their talent; what is missing is not headcount but this resonant atmosphere. Hence ICTS's founding principle is simple: hire only first-rate people, give them resources and freedom, and do not let them lower their ambitions.

1:11:19 AI can accelerate research but cannot make conceptual leaps
AI just won two Nobel Prizes in a row, but Gopakumar splits "AI for science" from "science for AI." The former he acknowledges as an overdrive gear—AI is accelerating a narrow class of tasks in research; yet the "theory" AI does today is far from his conceptual standard, since the best physics comes from conceptual leaps, not pattern recognition. Conversely, he is more optimistic about science for AI: among those who discovered scaling laws at Anthropic are people with physics backgrounds; Hopfield himself is a statistical physicist who used simple physics models to simulate the brain. Along this path, physicists may join computer scientists and neuroscientists to move AI from language models to physics-inspired world models. This distinction is worth remembering.

1:21:32 After the synthesizability filter, AI's new materials number zero
The most sobering cold water of the session came from audience Q&A: Google claims AI has discovered a large number of new materials, but after filtering for feasibility and synthesizability, Gopakumar says, "I think left with zero." His stance is not to dismiss AI materials science (someone in the room cited Microsoft's example of a DFT model with only 385,000 parameters that bypasses traditional hybrid methods), but to remind that the whole chain is long: after predicting a crystal structure, you still need to grow it and scale it, and each step can filter out surprises. He says India should also bet on this chain. This statement is a useful counter-calibration for the "AI discovers new materials" narrative.

item.title: AI Leaders Are Refineries, Not Native-App Winners
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-zhangxiaojun-ai没有安全巨头-公司制度将消亡/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-zhangxiaojun-ai没有安全巨头-公司制度将消亡/
item.description: AI enters the agent era: first-phase leaders are just refineries, not native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms, organizations shift from roles to tasks, and ultimately humans compete on creativity that creates something from nothing.
item.content:encoded:
AI enters the agent era: first-phase leaders are just refineries, not native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms, organizations shift from roles to tasks, and ultimately humans compete on creativity that creates something from nothing.

Zeng Ming offers a three-phase industrial history framework to give you a coordinate system for locating AI's current position—a cure for the optimism of 'this time it's different'—while also revealing the opportunity window for application entrepreneurs and the brutal expectations for giants in transition.

16:28 Building agents today is like building websites in 1992
Zeng Ming divides the industrialization of general-purpose technologies into three phases: first becoming social infrastructure, then an explosion of applications, and finally native applications. In 2026, token as a unit of measure reaching consensus signals the maturity of the first phase; the agent events around Chinese New Year (commonly called 'lobster') mark AI officially entering the agent era. He compares it to the website-building movement of 1992: back then people built websites to share information; today they build agents to share capabilities. The browser hasn't appeared yet; whoever can establish an agent standard and capture the user entry point may be the biggest opportunity in the next two years.

27:49 A ten-trillion-dollar company will emerge, but not these two
Zeng Ming states plainly that OpenAI and Anthropic are remarkable technical and commercial achievements, but business history shows that the first wave of companies to run fast are likely not the big winners of the native-application phase. Yahoo was worth $120 billion five years after founding, AOL reached a $220 billion valuation, yet neither became the Google of the next era. Model companies are more like AI cloud companies—refineries that extract base oil—while the real application value belongs to chemical plants and car companies—and cars were not built by oil companies. He believes a ten-trillion-dollar company will certainly appear, but it may not be the current leaders. Model companies will move toward an oligopoly plus heavy government regulation—a mature business.

1:10:29 The unit of AI-native organizations is tasks, not roles
Companies correspond to the industrial-age bureaucracy; AI disrupts the industrial age, so the corporate system will decay. The basic unit of an AI-native organization is not a role but a task: people are not organized by reporting lines but flow according to 'what problem needs solving,' with humans and AI collaborating around tasks. Thus well-designed jobs and hierarchies will disappear, and traditional middle management will die out. Future founders must first define the organization's task network. Silicon Valley's New Lab is a prototype of the new organizational form; OpenAI itself resembles a lab more than a traditional company. The culture of new organizations is more like a sports team, emphasizing transparency, sharing, and co-creation, not command and assessment.

1:31:32 Excellence is judged only in hindsight; being good is visible on the spot
Zeng Ming argues that 'being good ≠ being excellent.' Being good is growth sustained by positive feedback, while excellence requires overcoming repeated negative feedback, persisting when everyone disapproves, and ultimately proving oneself a prophet of the era through enormous success—so 'excellence is determined after the fact.' Those who are merely good easily fall into a cycle of self-validation, leading to conservative strategies. Excellent people have a small ego, tend to attribute success to the era and partners, and are mission-driven rather than externally valuation-driven. When identifying founders, he asks, 'What kind of self would you be satisfied with in ten years?' If the answer is 'a company worth ten billion dollars,' that is mainly ego-driven, not an inner mission. Truly excellent founders are often altruistic and empathetic.

1:47:24 Strategy in the AI era cannot be planned; it must be generated
In the AI era, strategy is not planning but generation. Zeng Ming proposes a 'strategy generation system': organizations must build an environment and network that allows strategic insights to emerge naturally. Because decision frequency is higher and quality demands are higher, CEOs cannot rely on linear extrapolation for planning, nor can they outsource strategy to McKinsey—McKinsey's rise was a product of the slow maturity of the industrial age. His methodology is 'look ten years, think three years, act one year,' with the core being 'think three years': you must see at least two or three milestones ahead, creating tension between short-term actions and the medium-term picture. Organizational building must ensure sufficient context rather than control, enabling the right people to make the right decisions at the right time.

2:01:39 The right analogy for robots is appliances, not cars
Zeng Ming believes robots are still in the strategic exploration phase, far from convergence. Two current routes—building a generalized brain first or closing the loop in specific scenarios—are both logically valid, and it's impossible to judge which will be faster in advance. Historically, the auto industry had thousands of companies from 1900 to 1920, and only when Ford built the assembly line in 1913 did it enter scale; robots haven't yet had their Model T moment, and whoever truly sells ten thousand robots will already be remarkable. But a better analogy for robots is appliances rather than cars: after electricity was invented, refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners, and countless other categories emerged. Robots interacting with the physical world will have N major scenarios—home, companionship, industry—each potentially spawning its own native giant.

2:03:39 Giants that feel safe are the least safe
Zeng Ming says that in the face of a giant wave, no one is safe; feeling safe is the most unsafe. In business history, no company has ever smoothly transitioned from one era to the next. IBM and Microsoft are the only two possible exceptions, and both are full of uncertainty. AI is a productivity revolution that disrupts the industrial revolution, not a continuation innovation like mobile internet, so the technological reserves and organizational culture of old giants are liabilities. Google can survive as an AI cloud company but may not capture the consumer entry point; ByteDance has an AI cloud opportunity, but Doubao is not the future application; Tencent's social relationships will be restructured; Alibaba is not naturally safe either. New platforms will most likely be created by new companies.

2:20:56 Human value lies in creating from nothing, not writing songs or painting
Borrowing Drucker's framework, Zeng Ming defines the AI era as the era of creativity: any knowledge work that can be structured will be taken over by AI. Humans are both forced and finally liberated to develop new potential. That potential is creativity—not writing songs or painting, but the ability to originally define complex problems and create something from nothing. AI has already taken all existing knowledge; human value lies in creating what does not yet exist. Hence he calls his mission 'being a happy researcher' and believes civilization's next step will reorganize around creativity, even forcing the education system to shift from 'knowledge indoctrination' to 'open exploration,' because young people already know the old path leads nowhere.

item.title: The Moat in AI Writing Isn't the Model—It's the Proprietary Data You Feed It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-aiandi-ai-写作的护城河不是模型-而是你喂进去的独家数据/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-aiandi-ai-写作的护城河不是模型-而是你喂进去的独家数据/
item.description: Over two years, writer Katie turned ChatGPT from a career coach during unemployment into a one-person content engine and a compounding editor. The core method isn't prompt tricks—it's using proprietary experience to fill the 'last mile' the model can't reach.
item.content:encoded:
Over two years, writer Katie turned ChatGPT from a career coach during unemployment into a one-person content engine and a compounding editor. The core method isn't prompt tricks—it's using proprietary experience to fill the 'last mile' the model can't reach.

Not a tool review, but how a non-technical writer turned AI into a mode of production. The meat is in the last 30 minutes; the earlier personal story provides motivational context.

2:09 An AI coach's biggest value isn't saving money
After being laid off, she was in a low point and couldn't afford a human career coach's hourly rate, but a $20/month ChatGPT subscription was acceptable. She found that writing out her thoughts and having AI question and push back from the outside helped her externalize thinking, counter catastrophizing, and gave her a sense of accountability. The most important legacy of this experience wasn't saving money—it was convincing her that AI can actually drive concrete change in life. At the time, she was hesitating about accepting Every's freelance offer, and ChatGPT nudged her to just try it.

8:26 Output comes from upfront context, not clever prompts
She once took on 8 blog posts, 3 ebooks, 24 LinkedIn posts, 24 X posts, and 16 Instagram posts in a week and a half. She did it not by writing smarter one-line prompts, but by doing extensive upfront context engineering: feeding the model brand info, product details, audience personas, and differentiators all at once. Much of the demand was essentially content reuse, and AI excels at rewriting a long article into versions for different platforms. Her rule: set up the scene early, and you can run fast later.

11:28 Give the model a fence before talking tone and word choice
Before Claude Projects existed, she had to store persistent documents in Google Docs and manually copy-paste them into context each time. This structure didn't come out of nowhere—it's the style guide tradition in content marketing: first define who the audience is, what their pain points are, how the product addresses them, who the competitors are, and where the differences lie. She says this gives the model a fenced playground, ensuring it won't go off track before you even discuss word choice, tone, and reading level. When Projects launched, she created a separate project for each client and each column.

15:40 The last mile of AI writing can only be filled by humans
She believes there's a 'last mile' problem in AI writing: models have knowledge cutoffs and don't live in the physical world. So the human's job is to supply the latest data and real experience that AI can't reach. She warns that if you just toss 'write a blog post about style guides' at the model, you'll get generic content it already knows—commodity information. What makes writing unique is fresh ingredients the model hasn't seen: internal company research, third-party reports, personal experience. The writing system is the kitchen; humans supply the good ingredients.

22:50 AI's value is reducing friction, not speeding up output
She openly discusses her bipolar disorder and points out that AI's value isn't just producing content faster—it's reducing friction in life. She put off booking a primary care physician for three years, then had Codex find a doctor who accepted her insurance and new patients, and complete the appointment. Email is pre-filtered by automation, so only messages that truly need a human reply reach her inbox. She says this completely solved her email anxiety. This isn't using AI as a production tool, but as assistive technology that makes her daily operation as a person easier.

27:03 Let AI interview you repeatedly so it can prioritize for you
Two years ago she simply asked ChatGPT 'can you be my career coach'; today that coach lives in a Codex project containing her job profile, Every's brand positioning, content performance data, a reader praise folder, and OKRs. She doesn't maintain a dashboard herself; she uses voice conversations to have the system prioritize by highest impact, and the system maintains the Kanban for her. The key to building this system was letting AI interview her repeatedly, then distilling those interviews into context. She says it's like having a Chief of Staff, not just a writer.

32:27 Feedback that only fixes the current draft is wasted
The Compound Writing plugin is built on a compounding mindset: every piece of feedback you give AI should flow back into the system so the next output automatically improves. She forked Kieran Klassen's Compound Engineering plugin and adapted it for writing: code and writing share the same stages—brainstorming, planning, drafting, review—except writing focuses more on structure, voice, and evidence. Editing is further split into a substantive edit that looks at big structure and argument, a line edit that handles sentence-by-sentence, and a final pass for publication checks. Now she doesn't write in a web chat window; she feeds the day's fresh material into this system.

39:19 Vonnegut as editor offers perspective, not verdicts
She built Vonnegut's eight narrative elements, Hitchcock's suspense principle about the bomb under the table, and Sorkin's and Sedaris's expression styles into the plugin as editing skills. Vonnegut checks whether the story starts as close to the end as possible and whether every sentence earns its place; Hitchcock's lens asks whether the reader will want to keep reading. She stresses this isn't about having a master's soul critique your draft—it's giving you a new perspective you can accept or reject. Non-professional writers might benefit even more because they're less likely to nitpick themselves while writing.
